profiles.meeting_scenario: A weekly coordination meeting between the reinforcement learning research lead and the distributed ML systems engineer on a reproduction of the original asynchronous Distributed Deep Q-Learning setup for an internal Atari-style visual control benchmark. They are preparing a Friday handoff where the research side wants a reference result for the milestone deck and the systems side wants the distributed training path to become the default launch path on the shared cluster. The agenda is to align on what exactly will count as the 'baseline run,' which checkpoint Maya will evaluate from, what 'stable by Friday' means for the handoff, and what components are implicitly included when they say the next run will use the 'distributed trainer.' The expected outcome is apparent agreement on the run configuration, artifact handoff, and Friday status update, even though subtle second-order assumptions remain unspoken.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Deep reinforcement learning, DQN variants, evaluation protocol design, visual control benchmarks
members.background: Maya leads the algorithmic reproduction effort for the lab's classic deep RL benchmark track and previously published on value-based learning from image observations; she is comfortable reasoning about replay dynamics, target-network behavior, and score curves, but relies on partner teams for cluster execution details.
members.private_state: She wants a Friday result that remains scientifically comparable to the single-node reference experiment she already validated, and she is worried that infrastructure defaults will quietly change the learning dynamics enough to make the distributed result unusable as a clean reproduction point.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says the 'baseline run,' they mean the canonical reproduction recipe from her experiment sheet, including the same learner-side hyperparameters as the validated single-node reference run, with distribution affecting execution scale rather than the effective training recipe.

A 'baseline' can still be distributed, but only if optimizer cadence, replay freshness, batch size, target-network sync interval, and update-to-data ratio remain functionally matched to the reference setup she already trusts.

The 'latest checkpoint' for Friday naturally means the latest checkpoint from the canonical single-node reference run that the milestone deck has been implicitly anchored to, because that is the cleanest comparison point unless someone explicitly says they are switching the reference line.
If the distributed trainer is described as 'stable,' that implies the learning behavior is not obviously distorted relative to the validated reference experiment, not just that the job stays up.
Saying they will 'switch to the distributed trainer' means keeping the learner semantics intact while moving execution onto the cluster.

members.name: Arjun Patel
members.expertise: Asynchronous training systems, parameter-server architectures, experiment orchestration, artifact pipelines
members.background: Arjun adapted an internal DistBelief-like stack to support reinforcement learning workloads, focusing on actor-learner job reliability, shared-cluster throughput, and standardized logging/checkpoint interfaces for long-running experiments.
members.private_state: He wants the team to stop treating the single-node reference path as the operational default and to converge on one launchable distributed configuration that uses the cluster's standard defaults, because maintaining special-case experiment handling right before the milestone is risky and time-consuming.
hidden_assumptions: When people refer to the 'baseline run' in a coordination meeting, they mean the standard distributed launch configuration that the team intends to use going forward, including the infrastructure-approved defaults for worker count, gradient aggregation, and per-update batch sizing.

A baseline is still a valid baseline as long as it is the agreed full-length training job for the benchmark game; matching every learner-side hyperparameter from an old single-node reference is less important than having one reproducible default path on the cluster.

The 'latest checkpoint' naturally means the newest checkpoint produced by the distributed pipeline that is now becoming the default artifact source, because once a workstream handoff happens, downstream consumers should stop reading from ad hoc reference-run directories.
If the distributed trainer is 'stable,' that means workers, replay services, parameter-server sync, checkpoint writes, and throughput are operationally reliable for the intended runtime.
Saying they will 'switch to the distributed trainer' includes the queueing, replay sharding, async gradient buffering, and checkpoint hooks already bundled into the production cluster path.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the baseline run
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree that Friday's handoff should use the 'baseline run.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means a distributed execution of the canonical reproduction recipe, preserving the validated single-node learner hyperparameters and training semantics closely enough that it serves as the scientific reference baseline.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the team's standard full-length distributed launch configuration, which uses infrastructure-default settings such as the normal async worker count and throughput-oriented batch/update settings, and is baseline because it is the default operational path.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are talking about a real full benchmark run rather than an obvious smoke test, so nothing sounds incompatible on the surface; 'baseline' feels like a settled shared term, while the hidden disagreement is about whether baseline is anchored to prior scientific comparability or to the default distributed configuration.

misalignment_points.topic: Which run the latest checkpoint comes from
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Maya will evaluate the 'latest checkpoint' on Friday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the latest checkpoint from the canonical single-node reference run that the milestone deck and prior score discussions have implicitly treated as the comparison anchor.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the latest checkpoint emitted by the newly adopted distributed pipeline run in the shared artifact bucket, because he assumes the handoff implies that path is now the official source.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both runs already exist in the project and both have plausible claims to being the obvious reference artifact; because teams often say 'latest checkpoint' once a path seems socially established, neither thinks to restate which run family the phrase is anchored to.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss wanting the distributed trainer to be 'stable by Friday.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the learning dynamics should look scientifically stable: no obvious Q-value blow-up, no suspicious drift from the reference learning curve, and scores in the expected range after enough frames.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the system should be operationally stable: workers remain healthy, throughput is consistent, replay and parameter servers do not stall, and checkpoints/logs are written reliably.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both criteria are desirable and commonly summarized by the same adjective in cross-functional ML meetings; since neither expects the other to object to 'stability,' the word creates false consensus instead of triggering clarification.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in switching to the distributed trainer
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the next run will 'use the distributed trainer.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this means her validated DQN learner will simply run in distributed execution, with the same effective replay/update semantics and only minimal wrapping for cluster launch and artifact handling.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this includes the full production stack he already packaged for RL workloads: sharded replay service, async gradient buffering, queue-based actor ingestion, standard checkpoint hooks, and the usual launch wrapper.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a straightforward infrastructure handoff, and both sincerely believe they are talking about the same code path; the hidden mismatch is about the boundary of what components are considered part of the trainer versus merely execution machinery.
